props.title: Tesis

sections.content: **Tesis** (1996) marked Alejandro Amenábar's explosive directorial debut, setting a new standard for Spanish thriller cinema. This meta-horror masterpiece follows film student Angela researching violence in media, only to uncover a snuff film ring operating within her university. The film brilliantly predated the found footage explosion of **The Blair Witch Project** (1999) and anticipated our modern obsession with extreme content and viral videos. Amenábar's razor-sharp critique of media violence feels even more relevant today, while his masterful building of suspense rivals early Hitchcock.

sections.content: The influence of **Tesis** ripples through later Spanish horror, particularly in works like **[REC]** (2007) and **Sleep Tight** (2011). Amenábar's exploration of voyeurism and complicity laid groundwork for films like **Funny Games** (1997) and **Cache** (2005), which similarly force viewers to confront their relationship with on-screen violence. The film's academic setting and meta-commentary on film studies prefigured similar themes in **Scream 2** (1997) and **The Cabin in the Woods** (2012).

What sets **Tesis** apart is its prescient understanding of how technology enables and amplifies violence. While predecessors like **Henry: Portrait of a Serial Killer** (1986) explored documented violence, **Tesis** specifically examines the role of academic analysis and media consumption in perpetuating cycles of violence. This theme would later be explored in films like **Nightcrawler** (2014) and **Christine** (2016). SUBHEAD: Impact on Found Footage and Meta-Horror

sections.content: **Tesis** helped establish conventions that would define found footage horror, though it isn't strictly part of that subgenre. Its influence can be seen in films like **Lake Mungo** (2008) and **Sinister** (2012), which similarly use discovered footage as plot devices while maintaining traditional narrative structures. The film's academic framing device would later be echoed in movies like **The House That Jack Built** (2018) and **Berberian Sound Studio** (2012), which use film industry settings to examine violence and art.
